title: When Should You Prop Up a Weak Team Member
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article lays out a structured framework for deciding whether to invest extra support in an underperforming team member. Three criteria matter most: the underperformance must stem from a skill gap or unclear expectations rather than attitude, the person must be genuinely coachable, and the role can't be so critical that the team can't absorb temporary weaker performance. Crucially, the piece insists this isn't purely the leader's call, since colleagues who must shoulder extra work deserve a say in whether the arrangement is worth it. It closes by warning that support without clear time bounds and milestones risks breeding resentment and dependency.
points: Propping up a weak performer only makes sense if the gap is skill-based, not attitude-based
The team member must be genuinely coachable and open to feedback for the investment to pay off
Colleagues who must cover the gap deserve input on whether the arrangement is worth the cost
Support needs explicit time bounds and milestones, or it risks breeding dependency and resentment
quotes: The decision to prop up and support a weak team member is a dilemma all leaders wrestle with at some point.
First, it is important that the underperformance stems from a skill gap or unclear expectations rather than a poor attitude.
Second, the team member must show they are coachable, open to feedback, and have a strong desire to improve.
If the effort results in dependency or decreased accountability, investing in this team member will erode trust and create jealousy within the team.
Leaders who make this call without input from the team members who must carry the weight stand a good chance of creating bitterness and resentment.
